# Known intentional Redis compatibility divergences.
#
# Format:
# <suite/test/command> :: <reason-category> :: <short reason>
#
# Reason categories:
# - feature-killed-per-A.11
# - mako-design-difference
# - mako-correctness-fix
#
KEYS/SCAN/DBSIZE set visibility :: mako-design-difference :: Set members are stored as hidden length-prefixed composite keys outside the visible `table_key_` namespace. Exposing set logical keys through keyspace enumeration needs a shared logical-key index or safe remote-scan design, not a local composite-prefix scan.
KEYS/SCAN/DBSIZE list visibility :: mako-design-difference :: Lists are stored as hidden meta/element composite keys outside the visible `table_key_` namespace. Exposing list logical keys through keyspace enumeration needs a shared logical-key index or safe remote-scan design, not a local composite-prefix scan.
KEYS/SCAN/DBSIZE sorted-set visibility :: mako-design-difference :: Sorted sets are stored as hidden member/score/meta composite keys outside the visible `table_key_` namespace. Exposing zset logical keys through keyspace enumeration needs a shared logical-key index or safe remote-scan design, not a local composite-prefix scan.
makoConMultiTrd extended Redis commands :: mako-design-difference :: Project decision: keep the alternate MultiTrd binary ABI-compatible only. Redis correctness is claimed for `third-party/redis/cpp/makoCon.cc`; making MultiTrd a correctness target would require executor deduplication and is not needed for this PR.
FLUSHDB/FLUSHALL :: mako-design-difference :: `FLUSHDB` clears the connection's selected logical database and `FLUSHALL` clears all sixteen, as in Redis. Neither is mapped onto a Mako DB namespace: the sixteen databases are one Mako keyspace partitioned by a hidden key prefix (see "Logical databases"), so both commands are a keyspace scan that deletes the keys belonging to the database being cleared, under the keyspace-exclusive lock. A `FLUSHDB` on database n therefore costs a walk of the whole keyspace, not of database n alone.
BITOP destination type :: mako-design-difference :: BITOP writes its result only when the destination is absent or a string; a destination holding another type returns WRONGTYPE instead of being overwritten as Redis does. Overwriting would need the SET path's collection-replacement logic in the executor.
OBJECT ENCODING/REFCOUNT :: mako-design-difference :: Mako stores no Redis object encodings or refcounts. OBJECT ENCODING reports the canonical large-object encoding per type (raw, quicklist, hashtable, skiplist) and REFCOUNT is always 1; FREQ and IDLETIME return errors because access time is not tracked.
MEMORY USAGE :: mako-design-difference :: Reported as key bytes + serialized value bytes + a fixed per-key overhead, in the spirit of Redis's estimate; SAMPLES is accepted and ignored.
RESTORE hash payload :: mako-design-difference :: Restoring a hash payload merges into an existing hash at the key (pre-existing behavior). String, set, and sorted-set payloads replace the key. REPLACE is accepted but the BUSYKEY check is not performed.
SPUBLISH/SSUBSCRIBE :: mako-design-difference :: Sharded Pub/Sub is served from the same single-keyspace registry as classic Pub/Sub, so it is correct only within one makoCon process, like classic Pub/Sub.
SLOWLOG/LATENCY/ACL :: mako-design-difference :: Compatibility shims for monitoring tools and client libraries: SLOWLOG and LATENCY report empty data, and ACL exposes a single implicit 'default' user that cannot be modified.
PFADD/PFCOUNT/PFMERGE sketch format :: mako-design-difference :: HyperLogLog sketches use a private dense format (16-byte header "MHLL" + version 1, then 16384 one-byte registers) stored as an ordinary string value, not Redis's "HYLL" header with its sparse/dense encodings. TYPE/DEL/EXPIRE/DUMP/RESTORE/GET therefore work unchanged, but a sketch cannot be copied byte-for-byte between Redis and Mako, PFDEBUG/PFSELFTEST are not offered, and there is no sparse representation, so every sketch costs 16400 bytes. Hash, register placement and estimator are Redis's, so an RDB-compatible export would only need a header and encoding translation.
PFCOUNT caching :: mako-design-difference :: Redis caches the last cardinality in the sketch header and invalidates it on PFADD. Mako recomputes the estimate on every PFCOUNT, so PFCOUNT never writes and is classified read-only; the cost is one pass over 16384 registers per key.
BITFIELD offset limit :: mako-design-difference :: The bit-offset parser shared with BITFIELD_RO rejects an offset whose field would end past bit 2^32; Redis instead rejects only offsets whose byte index reaches proto-max-bulk-len (512 MB), so it accepts the last few offsets of that range and grows the string past 512 MB. Both refuse anything larger, with the same error text.
BITFIELD integer arguments :: mako-design-difference :: Bit widths, offsets, values and increments go through the adapter's Rust integer parser (as BITCOUNT/BITPOS/BITFIELD_RO already do), which accepts spellings Redis's string2ll rejects, such as a leading plus or leading zeros (`u08`, `007`). Accepted spellings produce the value Redis computes for the canonical form; anything genuinely malformed still gets Redis's exact error text.
GEOSEARCH FROMMEMBER / GEORADIUSBYMEMBER atomicity :: mako-design-difference :: The center member's score is read by a request of its own, then the neighbor-box range reads go out as a second request. A request's op list is built before it is handed to the executor, so a range read cannot depend on a score read in the same request. The nine range reads are still one consistent snapshot; only the center position can be one write stale, which at most shifts the searched boxes if that member moved between the two requests. Inside MULTI the same lookup happens when the command is queued rather than at EXEC, so the queued command carries an already-resolved center.
Redis modules cannot be loaded :: mako-design-difference :: MODULE is recognized so a client library can ask and get a usable answer, but this adapter has no Redis module ABI and nothing below makoCon provides one, so no module can ever be loaded. MODULE LIST is an empty array, which is the truth rather than an emulation; MODULE LOAD and MODULE LOADEX answer Redis's own "Error loading the extension. Please check the server logs."; MODULE UNLOAD answers "Error unloading module: no such module with that name". Redis's tests/unit/moduleapi is excluded from the TCL scope for the same reason.
GEOSEARCHSTORE and MULTI :: mako-design-difference :: GEOSEARCHSTORE (and the STORE/STOREDIST forms of GEORADIUS and GEORADIUSBYMEMBER) cannot join the one operation list a MULTI hands the executor, because its write is decided by its own reads. A MULTI that queues one therefore runs the whole queue command by command inside a single interactive session and commits once, instead of on the batch path. The transaction is still all-or-nothing and every reply is byte-identical, but two things follow from the session: the chunked DBSIZE and FLUSHDB paths do not exist there, so a MULTI that mixes GEOSEARCHSTORE with DBSIZE or FLUSHDB answers DBSIZE from the general scan branch and cannot run FLUSHDB at all; and an optimistic-concurrency abort re-runs every queued command rather than the single batched request.
GEOSEARCHSTORE with both STORE and STOREDIST :: mako-design-difference :: Redis lets a second STORE or STOREDIST token on GEORADIUS silently replace the destination the first one named. Here the second one is a syntax error, so a destination is never dropped without the client hearing about it. Redis's own tests/unit/geo.tcl has no case for it.
GEOSEARCH cell selection :: mako-design-difference :: Which geohash cells a search reads is taken from the search area's bounding box rather than from Redis's fixed nine neighbor boxes, at the step Redis's geohashEstimateStepsByRadius (plus its decrease-step correction) chooses, dropping the step further while the box would span more than three cells per axis. Redis's latitude term is a coarse approximation it documents as such, and nine boxes miss points near the poles; its own tests/unit/geo.tcl "oblique direction" and "crossing pole" cases fail against a nine-box implementation and pass here. Cells are read center-first in Redis's neighbor order so an unsorted reply keeps Redis's ordering, and a search needing more than 16 cells reads the whole score space once instead, which is cheaper in this executor than many range ops.
GEOPOS/WITHCOORD coordinate digits :: mako-design-difference :: Coordinates are formatted from an f64 with "%.17f" and trailing zeros trimmed, in the shape of Redis's ld2string(LD_STR_HUMAN); Redis computes them as a long double, so the last few digits can differ. The value is the center of the same 52-bit geohash box, so the two agree far inside the ~0.6 m precision of the encoding itself.
Hash field expiry is eager on access :: mako-design-difference :: Redis keeps an expired hash field stored until its active-expire cycle or a command that touches that exact field removes it, so HLEN counts expired fields, EXISTS still reports the key, and an HSCAN page can come back empty. This adapter has no background expire cycle, so every hash read path drops the fields whose time has passed before answering: HLEN, EXISTS and TYPE see the hash as Redis sees it after active expiry, never before. Redis's tests/unit/type/hash-field-expire.tcl asserts the pre-expiry view in "Lazy Expire - fields are lazy deleted", "Lazy Expire - HLEN does count expired fields", "Test HSCAN with mostly expired fields return empty result" and the tail of "Test RENAME hash with fields to be expired"; every other semantic assertion in that file passes.
HEXPIRE NX/XX/GT/LT combinations :: mako-design-difference :: Redis reads exactly one condition token between the time and FIELDS, so a second one makes it report the FIELDS position error. The adapter looks at the token after the condition as well, and when the pair cannot be combined it answers Redis's own "NX and XX, GT or LT options at the same time are not compatible" or "GT and LT options at the same time are not compatible"; a pair Redis would accept elsewhere, such as XX GT, still gets the FIELDS position error.
DUMP/RESTORE of hash field expirations :: mako-design-difference :: The MAKO_HASH_DUMP payload carries fields and values only, so a DUMP/RESTORE round trip loses the per-field expirations, as a RESTORE onto a key does. Carrying them would change the private dump format, which the phase-2 DUMP/RESTORE divergence already records as not byte-compatible with Redis.
Hash statistics for field expirations :: mako-design-difference :: INFO does not report the `expired_subkeys` counter or the `subexpiry` field of INFO keyspace that Redis added with hash field expiration, in the spirit of the other observability shims.
Keyspace enumeration inside a transaction :: mako-design-difference :: KEYS, SCAN, DBSIZE and RANDOMKEY scan storage, so inside one MULTI they see the keyspace as it stood when the transaction began: a key an earlier command in the same transaction created is missing, because its write is still in the executor's pending_writes buffer, and a key an earlier command deleted is still listed, because its removal is still in pending_deletes. Both buffers are flushed once, just before Commit, because STO built with -DREAD_MY_WRITES=OFF cannot take a second write, or a delete, of a record the same transaction created: MassTrans::install() re-publishes the value the record was created with and MassTrans::transDelete() on it takes the `if (!valid) Sto::abort()` branch. Redis would show the transaction its own changes. Every other read path does: the string, hash, set, list and zset reads all consult the buffers, so only enumeration is stale. Before the buffering these sequences failed the whole transaction instead, which reached the client as "ERR backend".
CLUSTER single-node emulation :: mako-design-difference :: `MAKO_REDIS_CLUSTER_MODE=emulated` makes one makoCon describe itself as a one-node cluster owning slots 0-16383, in the spirit of Dragonfly's emulated cluster mode, so client libraries that will only speak to a cluster can build a slot map and connect. Nothing is actually sharded: there is one keyspace, one node and one shard, so no key is ever MOVED or ASK-redirected, slot ownership never changes, CLUSTER FORGET/MEET/SETSLOT/ADDSLOTS/REPLICATE/FAILOVER/RESET and the rest of the administrative subcommands are not offered (they get the unknown-subcommand error), and the epochs and message counters CLUSTER INFO reports are constants. READONLY and READWRITE steer reads at replicas in a real cluster; with one master and no replicas there is nothing to steer, so both simply reply OK. The default mode is `off`, where CLUSTER, READONLY and READWRITE all answer "ERR This instance has cluster support disabled" and INFO reports cluster_enabled:0, which is what the adapter did before the emulation existed.
CLUSTER COUNTKEYSINSLOT/GETKEYSINSLOT :: mako-design-difference :: Both answer as though the node held no keys: COUNTKEYSINSLOT returns 0 and GETKEYSINSLOT an empty array, for any in-range slot. Answering truthfully would mean a full keyspace scan per call plus a CRC16 of every key, and this executor answers enumeration by scanning storage; with a single node owning every slot the answer carries no routing information anyway. An out-of-range slot still gets Redis's "ERR Invalid slot".
CLUSTER SLOTS node entry :: mako-design-difference :: The node triple is [ip, port, id]; Redis 7 appends a fourth element, an array of extra networking metadata, which is empty for a node with no announced hostname. Clients read the first three positions and ignore the rest.
CLUSTER node id :: mako-design-difference :: Redis picks a random 40-hex-character node id once and remembers it in nodes.conf. This server has no such file, so the id is derived deterministically from the advertised host:port with five seeded FNV-1a passes. It is the right shape and constant for a given address across restarts and across calls, but it is not random and carries no cryptographic claim; two nodes emulating a cluster at the same advertised address would collide, which single-node emulation cannot produce.
MONITOR scope :: mako-design-difference :: A monitor sees only the commands this makoCon front-end process runs, the same limit classic and sharded Pub/Sub already carry: the registry is a process-global list, not a shared one, so a deployment with several front ends needs a monitor on each. Commands that reach Mako storage from anywhere other than this process are invisible to it.
MONITOR command coverage :: mako-design-difference :: Every command this adapter recognizes is reported. Redis leaves out the ones flagged CMD_ADMIN or CMD_SKIP_MONITOR, so a real server hides CONFIG, DEBUG, SLOWLOG, CLIENT KILL and the rest of its administrative set from the monitor stream; this one shows them. A command Redis would reject before executing is not reported here either: the feed sits after the parse, so an unknown command or a wrong-arity call produces its error and no line, as in Redis. Credentials are redacted as Redis redacts them, for AUTH and for HELLO's AUTH clause; Redis also redacts MIGRATE's AUTH/AUTH2 arguments, and MIGRATE is not offered here.
MONITOR database field :: mako-design-difference :: The `[<db> <addr>]` field reports the issuing connection's selected database, as Redis does. Redis also prints `[<db> lua]` for each command a script issued; here a script's commands do not reach the monitor feed at all, so a monitor sees the EVAL and not the commands inside it.
MONITOR and the raw GET/SET fast path :: mako-design-difference :: While at least one monitor is attached, the raw GET/SET fast frame path declines every frame and the general parser handles it, so those two commands are reported like all the others. The gate is one relaxed atomic load of the monitor count at the entry of that path, so with no monitor attached the path and its cost are exactly what they were. Attaching a monitor therefore slows every client on the server, not only the monitored traffic; Redis has no equivalent shortcut to give up, but it too pays for monitors on every command.
Logical databases :: mako-design-difference :: Redis's sixteen databases are emulated inside one Mako keyspace. Database 0 keys are stored under exactly the bytes the client sends, so the layout of every keyspace that existed before is byte-for-byte unchanged, and a key in database 1..15 is stored under the hidden prefix `0x02 <db as one byte> ':'` applied to the Redis-visible name before any storage prefix (`table_key_`, the 0x01 collection namespaces, the TTL metadata). Every type, TTL, WATCH, lock stripe and DUMP/RESTORE mechanism therefore works per database without knowing databases exist. Real Redis keeps sixteen independent dictionaries, so a database there costs nothing to enumerate; here KEYS, SCAN, DBSIZE, RANDOMKEY and FLUSHDB on database n are all prefix scans of the single keyspace.
Reserved first byte 0x02 :: mako-design-difference :: A user key may not begin with byte 0x02, which gets the same "invalid key: reserved internal prefix" error that byte 0x01 has always got, because 0x02 introduces the logical-database prefix and database 0 would otherwise be able to spell another database's key. Redis allows any byte sequence as a key.
SELECT inside MULTI :: mako-design-difference :: Redis queues SELECT with the rest of the transaction and applies it at EXEC, so the commands queued after it still refer to the database that was selected when MULTI began. Here SELECT takes effect immediately, while it is queued, because a queued command's keys acquire their database prefix at parse time, which is the single place the prefix is applied. A MULTI that selects another database therefore executes the commands after the SELECT against that database. Everything else about MULTI/EXEC is unchanged, and a transaction that does not contain SELECT is identical.
INFO keyspace for databases 1..15 :: mako-design-difference :: INFO keyspace always reports db0 from the cached count it has always used, and reports databases 1..15 only when the server runs with MAKO_REDIS_INFO_ALL_DBS=1, and then only for databases holding at least one key. Redis reports every non-empty database, which costs it nothing because it holds a size per dictionary; counting a database here is a keyspace scan, so reporting all sixteen would turn every INFO scrape into sixteen scans. Each database's count is cached for two seconds, as db0's always has been.
MOVE :: mako-design-difference :: MOVE is one executor op that copies the whole object to the destination database's spelling of the name and deletes the source inside one Mako transaction, reusing COPY's per-type logic, so it carries strings, sets, lists, hashes, sorted sets, the key TTL and hash field expirations. It answers 0 when the source does not exist or the destination name is already taken, and errors with "source and destination objects are the same" for the current database and "DB index is out of range" outside 0..15, as Redis does. Because it is a copy and a delete rather than a pointer move, its cost is proportional to the size of the object, where Redis's is constant.
Logical databases and the raw GET/SET fast path :: mako-design-difference :: A connection that has selected a database other than 0 does not take the raw GET/SET fast frame path, because that path sends the key to storage without building a command and so never applies the database prefix. The gate is one field load beside the existing monitor gate, so a connection on database 0, which is every connection that never sends SELECT, keeps the path and its cost exactly as they were.
Lua scripting engine :: mako-design-difference :: EVAL/EVALSHA/EVAL_RO/EVALSHA_RO run on an embedded Lua 5.1 built from source through mlua (features lua51, vendored), which is the dialect Redis scripts are written against, but it is not Redis's own interpreter with Redis's patches. A fresh Lua state is created per call rather than one sandboxed state being reused, so no global a script defines can leak into the next script; the cost is one state construction per EVAL. The state is sandboxed to the library surface Redis allows -- string, table, math, cjson and os.clock/os.time/os.difftime -- so io, package, require, loadfile, dofile, load, loadstring, print, debug, coroutine and string.dump are all removed, and reading or creating an undeclared global is an error carrying Redis's own text. What Redis has that this does not is the read-only table: a script here can still overwrite redis.call or cjson.encode inside its own state, where Redis answers "Attempt to modify a readonly table"; a fresh state per call means that reaches no other script.
Script atomicity and retries :: mako-design-difference :: A script runs inside one interactive Mako transaction, so its effects are all-or-nothing and invisible until it returns. When the commit loses an optimistic-concurrency race everything the script produced is discarded and the whole script is re-run from scratch in a new transaction, up to 32 attempts, after which the client gets `ERR backend`. Redis never re-runs a script. Redis requires scripts to be deterministic, so a re-run is not observable for a conforming script, but a script that calls TIME, reads a random source, or has a side effect outside the keyspace can observe that it ran more than once.
Script keys and locking :: mako-design-difference :: The keys a script declares in KEYS are the ones whose lock stripes the script's transaction holds, so two scripts naming the same key are serialized. A key a script touches without declaring it is still correct, but it is protected only by optimistic concurrency, so a conflict on it appears as a re-run rather than as a wait. Redis has no such distinction because it executes one script at a time.
A busy script and the connections around it :: mako-design-difference :: A script occupies the worker thread that read its command, because Mako's per-thread state -- the open STO transaction and the thread's shard client -- belongs to that thread and a thread that has not been through the server's own thread_init cannot run a transaction at all. Redis has the same shape of problem and this follows its answer: until `lua-time-limit` the server simply does not answer that worker's other connections, and past it the script's own busy hook drains them on every tick, answering BUSY to everything that is not MULTI, a doomed EXEC or SCRIPT KILL, and still accepting new connections so a client that wants to kill the script can always get in. Connections on the other workers are unaffected throughout. What differs from Redis is the scope: Redis runs one script at a time for the whole server, while here one script per worker thread can run at once, so two scripts can be in flight together and each pumps only its own worker's connections.
SCRIPT KILL with concurrent scripts :: mako-design-difference :: Redis runs one script at a time, so SCRIPT KILL names an unambiguous script. This adapter can run one per worker thread, so SCRIPT KILL describes the set of running scripts: NOTBUSY when none is running, UNKILLABLE while any running script has already written, and otherwise it kills every running script that has not written yet.
Script error text :: mako-design-difference :: An error a script raises itself is reported in Redis's shape, `ERR user_script:<line>: <message> script: <sha>, on @user_script:1.`, with the line number coming from Lua. An error that a redis.call produced is passed through exactly as the command wrote it (WRONGTYPE, NOSCRIPT, the ERR texts), where Redis appends the same script context to it. Keeping the command's text unchanged is what lets a client match on the error code it would get outside a script.
Script library surface :: mako-design-difference :: redis.call, redis.pcall, redis.error_reply, redis.status_reply, redis.sha1hex, redis.log, redis.setresp, redis.breakpoint, redis.debug, redis.replicate_commands, redis.REDIS_VERSION/REDIS_VERSION_NUM (reported as 7.4.0) and a cjson table are provided, and the table is also bound to the Redis 7 name `server`. cmsgpack, struct and bit are not provided at all, so a script that uses them fails with the sandbox's "Script attempted to access nonexistent global variable" error. redis.setresp(2) is accepted and redis.setresp(3) is an error, because replies always reach a script in RESP2 shape.
cjson limits :: mako-design-difference :: cjson.encode/decode are a small JSON codec written for this adapter, not the Lua cjson module. JSON null decodes to Lua nil, where real cjson uses a lightuserdata sentinel; numbers decode as Lua numbers, so a very large integer loses precision exactly as a Lua 5.1 double does; an empty Lua table encodes as `{}`; a table holding both array and hash entries encodes as an object; a key that is neither a string nor a number is skipped rather than refused; and the module's configuration functions (encode_keep_buffer, encode_max_depth, decode_max_depth, encode_invalid_numbers, encode_sparse_array) do not exist, so the fixed limits are 64 levels of nesting for both directions.
Deeply nested script replies :: mako-design-difference :: A script can return a table that contains itself. The conversion stops at 128 levels of nesting and ends the reply with Redis's own `ERR reached lua stack limit`, where Redis stops at whatever depth its Lua C stack allows. Without the cap the conversion would recurse until the process stack gave out.
Commands refused inside a script :: mako-design-difference :: Besides the commands Redis itself refuses from a script (MULTI/EXEC/DISCARD, WATCH/UNWATCH, the SUBSCRIBE family, MONITOR, EVAL, SCRIPT, CLIENT, AUTH, HELLO, QUIT, RESET), this adapter also refuses SELECT with the same "This Redis command is not allowed from script" error, so a script always runs in the database its connection had selected when EVAL arrived, and it refuses any command that produces no reply of its own rather than listing them. The blocking pops behave as they do in Redis: they are allowed and do not block, because the script's transaction runs the pop and answers nil when there is nothing to pop.
PUBLISH from a script :: mako-design-difference :: A script's PUBLISH is buffered and delivered once the script's transaction commits, so a message is never seen for a script that failed. Its reply, the number of receivers, is the number of subscribers at the moment of the call rather than at the moment of delivery.
EVAL inside MULTI :: mako-design-difference :: Redis queues EVAL with the rest of a transaction and runs the script at EXEC. Here EVAL runs immediately, even between MULTI and EXEC, because a script opens its own interactive transaction and the queued-command path builds one operation list for the whole batch. A script is atomic on its own either way; what differs is that its writes are visible before the surrounding EXEC.
WATCH and a script's declared keys :: mako-design-difference :: A committed EVAL bumps the versions of the keys it declared in KEYS as well as the keys it actually wrote, so a WATCH on a declared key that the script only read is invalidated too. Redis invalidates a watch only for keys a command really modified. The direction is safe: a transaction aborts that Redis would have allowed, never the other way round.
Stream storage layout :: mako-design-difference :: A stream is five hidden composite-key families rather than Redis's radix tree of listpack macro nodes: one meta record per stream ("\x01X#:"), one record per entry ("\x01X:"), one per consumer group ("\x01XG:"), one per consumer ("\x01XC:") and one per pending-entry-list entry ("\x01XP:"). Entry and PEL keys end in the 128-bit ID written big-endian and fixed-width, so lexicographic key order is ID order and an XRANGE start/end pair is a storage key range. Nothing is delta-compressed and no entry shares a record with its neighbours, so a stream costs one storage record per entry where Redis costs one per ~100, and a DUMP payload is not byte-compatible with Redis's.
XADD/XTRIM approximate trimming :: mako-design-difference :: The `~` modifier is accepted and trims exactly to the threshold. Redis trims whole radix-tree macro nodes, so it stops early and leaves up to stream-node-max-entries more entries than asked for; trimming exactly satisfies the same contract (the stream is never longer than the threshold) but removes more than Redis would. LIMIT is honoured as a hard cap on the entries one call may remove, which is the guarantee its name states, rather than Redis's node-granular interpretation. Redis's own tests/unit/type/stream.tcl asserts the node-granular counts in "XADD with MAXLEN option and the '~' argument", "XADD with LIMIT delete entries no more than limit", "XADD with LIMIT consecutive calls", "XTRIM with ~ is limited" and "XTRIM with LIMIT delete entries no more than limit"; every other trimming assertion in that file passes.
XINFO radix-tree-keys and radix-tree-nodes :: mako-design-difference :: Reported as the number of entries currently stored and that number plus one. There is no radix tree here: each entry genuinely is one key in Mako's ordered index, so the entry count is the truthful answer to "how many keys does this stream occupy", while Redis counts macro nodes. Redis's own tests/unit/type/stream.tcl grows a stream until radix-tree-keys exceeds 20, which needs a number that rises with the length; a constant would loop forever.
XINFO STREAM and XSETID read the whole stream :: mako-design-difference :: Both need the largest ID still stored -- XINFO for last-entry, XSETID for the "smaller than the target stream top item" check -- and Mako's ordered index only scans forward, so both walk the entry range once. Redis reads its last macro node. XRANGE, XREAD and the trimming paths are unaffected: a forward read stops the walk at COUNT, and only XREVRANGE, which needs the last COUNT entries of its range, reads the range before it answers.
GET/APPEND/STRLEN/GETEX/GETDEL on a collection key :: mako-design-difference :: These five do not consult the executor's type guard, so against a key holding a list, set, sorted set, hash or stream, GET/GETEX answer nil, STRLEN answers 0, APPEND replaces the key with a string and GETDEL deletes it; Redis answers WRONGTYPE and leaves the key alone. GET runs through the executor's specialized string path, which this PR's performance claims rest on and which is therefore out of scope to change; the other four share its read helper. Every other string command does check the type: SET and SETEX replace the key as Redis does, and SETRANGE, GETRANGE, SETBIT, GETBIT, the INCR family, BITCOUNT, BITPOS, BITFIELD and BITFIELD_RO all answer WRONGTYPE. This is not specific to streams; it predates them and is recorded here because the stream tests are the first to assert it.
Blocking XREAD resolves $ and + in a read of its own :: mako-design-difference :: "$" and "+" name a position rather than an entry, and Redis fixes that position inside the command. A request's operation list is built before the executor runs it, so a blocking XREAD reads every named stream's last-generated ID in a request of its own, immediately before its first attempt, and parks the resolved IDs with the command. The position is therefore fixed once, when the command arrives, which is the semantics that matters: an XADD landing while the client is parked is delivered rather than skipped. What differs is that an XADD landing between the resolve and the first attempt is delivered by the first attempt instead of by the wake-up, which is indistinguishable to the client. A non-blocking XREAD needs no extra read: "$" asks for entries newer than the call, and nothing already stored can qualify.
Blocked stream readers are served in arrival order :: mako-design-difference :: Several clients blocked on the same stream are woken one at a time, in the order they blocked, because the blocked-client registry hands the retry turn to the front of each key's queue -- the same fairness rule BLPOP has always used here. The queue is per command class: a list or sorted-set pop hands one element to exactly one waiter, while a stream read takes nothing away, so the two classes take their turns independently and a pop that can never be served cannot starve the readers behind it (before that split, a BLPOP parked on a key that later became a stream held the front forever). For XREAD the ordering only delays delivery, because the entries stay in the stream and each client in turn reads the same ones; for XREADGROUP with ">" the first client takes the new entries and the others go back to waiting, which is what Redis does too.
Per-consumer pending-entry lists are derived :: mako-design-difference :: Redis keeps two radix trees per pending entry, the group's and the owning consumer's, and moves the entry between consumer trees on a claim. Here there is one record per pending entry, in the group's list, carrying the owner's name, and a per-consumer view is that list filtered by owner. A claim is therefore one record write instead of two tree operations, and XACK, XCLAIM and XAUTOCLAIM each touch one record per entry; the cost is that XPENDING for a single consumer, XREADGROUP's history replay and XINFO's per-consumer pending list all walk the group's list rather than a shorter one. Every count Redis reports is kept alongside (the group's PEL size and each consumer's pending count) so XINFO and XPENDING answer them without the walk.
XREADGROUP history bumps the delivery count :: mako-design-difference :: Replaying a consumer's pending entries with an explicit ID sets each replayed entry's delivery time to now and increments its delivery count, which is what Redis does, but Redis deliberately does not replicate that change and this adapter has no separate replication stream to leave it out of. An entry that is in the pending list but no longer in the stream is reported as its ID with a null field list and is left in the pending list, as in Redis; only XCLAIM and XAUTOCLAIM remove it.
XCLAIM FORCE delivery count :: mako-design-difference :: A pending entry that FORCE creates from nothing starts at delivery count 1 and is then incremented by the claim itself, so it is reported as 2 unless JUSTID or RETRYCOUNT was given. This is Redis's own arithmetic, kept deliberately rather than normalized to 1.
Very large write transactions :: mako-design-difference :: A MULTI holding a few thousand writing commands crashes the executor: a 5,000-command SET transaction is enough, and a 4,000-command XADD one still works, so the limit is in the storage transaction rather than in any command. A pipeline of 10,000 writes is fine, and so is a 5,000-command read-only MULTI; only the size of one transaction's write set matters. This predates streams -- plain SET reproduces it and nothing in the adapter's command paths is involved -- and fixing it means changing STO's write-set sizing below makoCon, which this PR does not touch. It is recorded here because Redis's own tests/unit/type/stream.tcl is the first in-scope file to build a transaction that large ("XADD mass insertion and XLEN", 10,000 XADDs in one MULTI), and it is why that file is run from a scratch copy that sends those entries as a pipeline instead. Diagnosed 2026-09-17 with gdb: STO's Transaction keeps its items in 64 chunks of 512 (tset_max_capacity = 32768, src/mako/sto/Transaction.hh); at item 32,769 refresh_tset_chunk indexes tset_[64], one past the array, and allocate_item writes through the garbage pointer. The bounds check is an assert in Transaction.cc that Release builds compile out. The boundary is exact and repeatable: GEOADD with 14,974 members in one command succeeds every time and 14,975 crashes every time (about 2.2 items per member), so it is not load-related. Fix options: an adapter-side guard that estimates the item count of an op list and answers with an error before executing, or a growable chunk array / clean abort inside STO. Also recorded as a comment on PR 72.
XREADGROUP counts a history replay as a change :: mako-design-difference :: Every XREADGROUP bumps the server's dirty counter, including a replay of a consumer's own pending entries, which does change their delivery time and delivery count. Redis decided those metadata changes are too small to propagate and leaves the counter alone, which its tests/unit/type/stream-cgroups.tcl asserts in "XREADGROUP from PEL does not change dirty". Here the counter also drives WATCH invalidation and the OOM check, so counting the replay is the conservative direction: a WATCH is invalidated that Redis would have allowed, never the other way round.
RESTORE of a Redis-produced stream payload :: mako-design-difference :: DUMP payloads are this adapter's private format for every type, so a stream payload produced by a real Redis cannot be restored here, and Redis's tests/unit/type/stream-cgroups.tcl "Loading from legacy (Redis <= v6.2.x, rdb_ver < 10) persistence" and its v7.0 companion fail with "DUMP payload version or checksum are wrong". A MAKO_STREAM_DUMP payload round-trips within this adapter, carrying the entries, the consumer groups, their consumers and their pending-entry lists.
Stream syntax errors :: mako-design-difference :: The stream commands answer a malformed option list with Redis's exact "ERR syntax error", where every other command in this adapter answers "ERR protocol error: syntax error" for the same class of mistake. Redis's tests/unit/type/stream.tcl matches the text exactly, and matching Redis is worth more on a new command surface than matching the adapter's older habit.
INFO clients blocking-key counters :: mako-correctness-fix :: INFO clients now reports Redis 7's `total_blocking_keys` and `total_blocking_keys_on_nokey`, counted from the blocked-client registry: the first is the number of keys some client is parked on, the second how many of those have a client waiting for the key itself to appear. XREADGROUP is the only command in that second class here, as it is in Redis, because a missing key or group answers NOGROUP rather than waiting.
INFO errorstats and commandstats :: mako-design-difference :: INFO does not report Redis's per-error `errorstat_<CODE>` section, its per-command `calls`/`failed_calls`/`rejected_calls` breakdown, or `total_error_replies`, so a test that asserts a failed command was counted cannot pass. Redis's tests/unit/type/stream-cgroups.tcl "XGROUP DESTROY should unblock XREADGROUP with -NOGROUP" is one: the unblock and its NOGROUP reply are correct, and only the three statistics assertions after them fail. This is the same observability scope the SLOWLOG/LATENCY/ACL shims sit in.
HRANDFIELD/ZRANDMEMBER sampling :: mako-design-difference :: HRANDFIELD and ZRANDMEMBER do not sample randomly. Each call reads the whole hash or sorted set and returns a consecutive window of fields or members starting at an offset taken from a process-wide counter that advances by one per call, wrapping around the end; the negative-count form repeats that walk instead of drawing with replacement. SPOP and SRANDMEMBER do use a per-thread random generator, without replacement for SPOP and positive counts and with replacement for negative counts. Found while documenting phase 3 (2026-09-24); the Redis TCL guard does not assert randomness for these two commands, so it passes either way.
